title: The neutral person
hook: the cashier, the neighbor, someone you barely notice

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dear friend, and the root of metta: mitta, a friend. Your line was friendship, widened. Did you try that easy goodwill on someone you barely know? Day one hundred and one.

Think about the last person who handed you a coffee. What did they look like? What color was their hair? Most of us have no idea. We pass dozens of people a day who are, to us, basically furniture. The bus driver. The person two desks over. The neighbor whose name you never caught. We don't dislike them. We just don't see them. Today's step in metta is exactly those people. Not the ones you love, not the ones who annoy you. The ones in the middle, who have somehow become invisible.
screen: `WHO HANDED YOU YOUR COFFEE?` → `PEOPLE AS FURNITURE.` → `THE ONES IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: In the Visuddhimagga's order, after yourself, a benefactor and a dear friend, comes the neutral person: someone you neither like nor dislike. And this step is harder than it sounds. With a friend, warmth is already there. With a neutral person, there's nothing to start from. So the practice asks you to build the wish on something true: this person wants to be happy, exactly as much as you do. They woke up this morning with their own worries. They have someone they love, something they're afraid of, a song they know every word to. They have a whole life, and you're seeing about four seconds of it. There's an old teaching in the Pali texts that makes the same point from a longer angle. The Buddha says the round of rebirth is so long that it's hard to find a being who hasn't, at some point, been your mother, your father, your brother, your sister, your child. Many Buddhists take that literally, and some hear it as a picture. Either way, the effect is the same. The stranger stops being a stranger. The manual gives a practical tip too, for whenever the feeling runs dry: go back to someone easier, like your friend, feel the warmth again, then return. Like warming your hands at a fire before going back out in the cold. And here's what people notice after a few weeks of this practice. The cashier starts to look like a person again. You remember a name. You look up. That's metta, working quietly, in the least dramatic place in your day.
screen: `NEITHER LIKED NOR DISLIKED.` · `THEY WANT TO BE HAPPY TOO.` · `NO STRANGERS IN A LONG ROUND.` · `WARM YOUR HANDS, THEN GO BACK.` · then, large: `THEY HAVE A WHOLE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you saw recently but don't really know: a cashier, a driver, a neighbor. You may not remember their face clearly; that's fine. Picture what you can. Remind yourself: they want to be happy, just like me. Then offer the phrases slowly. May you be safe. May you be happy. May you be healthy. May you live with ease. If it feels thin, think of your friend for a breath, and come back. The bell holds the time.
The neutral person. Someone you neither like nor dislike: the fourth step of metta, and the easiest to forget.
Your line: they have a whole life. Today, look up at one person who serves you, and silently wish them well. Day one hundred and one.

howItsDone: In the traditional order of metta practice, Buddhists extend the wishes to a neutral person, someone they neither like nor dislike, after themselves, a benefactor and a dear friend.

match.prompt: the steps so far — tap the pairs.

myth: the neutral person is easier than the dear friend
there's no warmth to start from, so you build the wish on what's true: they want to be happy too.
the manual says you can warm up with your friend and come back
when it gets thin, go back to the dear friend, then return.
the Pali texts say it's hard to find a being who hasn't been your mother
the round of rebirth is that long, so the stranger stops being a stranger.

fork.setup: you're sending metta to a stranger and it feels like nothing. what does the old manual suggest?
options: go back to your friend for a moment, then return.
fork.reveal: warm your hands at the fire: return to the dear friend, feel the warmth, then go back to the neutral person.

original.note: Pali: standing in the middle, neutral; the manual's word for the neutral person.

trapdoor: what you thought: be polite to strangers.
what it means: seeing that the person you barely notice has a whole life and wants to be happy.
what a scholar hears: SN 15.14–19 teach that in the long round it's hard to find a being who hasn't been one's mother, father, sibling or child; Visuddhimagga IX calls the neutral person majjhatta.

notes: The 'warm your hands' tip is a paraphrase of Visuddhimagga IX's advice to return to an easier person when the feeling fades; in the manual that advice is given mainly for the hostile person, so the script now frames it generally ('whenever the feeling runs dry'). Confirm it fits this stage.
SN 15.14–19 numbering (mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter); confirm.
Devanagari मज्झत्त for Pali majjhatta; please check.
